newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss president envisions big humanitarian fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss president envisions big humanitarian fund.

text.p: Swiss President Arnold Koller proposed Wednesday creating a huge humanitarian fund that would use Swiss official gold reserves to aid victims of human rights abuses, catastrophes and the Holocaust.

In a key address to parliament on Switzerland's role as a World War Two financial centre, Koller said the planned "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" underscored the Swiss humanitarian tradition and gratitude for having escaped two world wars.

If adopted, the fund could draw on around seven billion Swiss francs ($4.7 billion) in funds from official gold reserves and generate a few hundred million francs (dollars) a year for needy recipients in Switzerland and abroad, he said.

They could include "victims of poverty and catastrophes, of genocide and other serious human rights abuses, of course also for those of the Holocaust and Shoa," he said, in Berne's boldest response yet to charges the Swiss coldly profited from the war.

Koller reaffirmed neutral Switzerland's commitment to facing its history squarely as it reexamines its past and urged its critics to give a historians' panel conducting a sweeping historical review the time it needs to do its job properly.
But Koller also made clear Berne felt the need to affirm Switzerland's humanitarian traditions and its thanks that it was spared the misery of two devastating wars.

"In this sense the Federal Council (cabinet), in accord with the Swiss National Bank and with an eye on the anniversary year of 1998, has developed the idea of a Swiss Foundation for Solidarity," Koller said, referring to the 150th anniversary of the modern Swiss state next year.
He said the foundation could be financed by making more efficient use of the country's gold reserves, a process that will take some time and require amending the Swiss constitution.

If the plan is adopted, the government would not contribute any public funds to a Holocaust memorial fund, something right-wing politicians have attacked as tantamount to an admission of guilty behaviour during the war.
Spurred by international pressure, big Swiss banks have already donated 100 million francs ($67 million) to such a fund.
The Swiss National Bank (SNB), which has acknowledged buying looted gold from Nazi Germany, also plans to contribute 100 million francs, Koller said.

SNB Chairman Hans Meyer said the new plan entailed selling gold over a 10-year period, but insisted such sales -- worth "several billion" Swiss francs -- would not have to disrupt the gold market and would not undermine the currency's stability.
